meta.title: Foro de São Paulo — Cronologia
meta.subtitle: Chronology of the São Paulo Forum (1990–present)
meta.description: An open, source-referenced chronology of the meetings of the Foro de São Paulo (São Paulo Forum), the conference of left-wing political parties and organizations of Latin America and the Caribbean, founded in 1990.
meta.dataQualityNote: This is a work-in-progress dataset compiled from public secondary sources (see references). Meeting host cities and years are well attested; exact dates and edition (roman-numeral) numbers vary between sources and are marked as unverified where appropriate. The full list of all 48 founding organizations is not yet fully sourced. Contributions and corrections against primary sources are welcome.

founding.venue: Hotel Danúbio (now defunct), central São Paulo
founding.originalName: Encontro de Partidos e Organizações de Esquerda da América Latina e do Caribe (Meeting of Left and Anti-imperialist Parties and Organizations of Latin America and the Caribbean)
founding.renamed: Adopted the name 'Foro de São Paulo' from the 1991 Mexico City meeting onward, in reference to the location of the first meeting.
founding.convenedBy: Initiative of the Brazilian Workers' Party (Partido dos Trabalhadores, PT), led by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
founding.context: Convened after the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of the Soviet bloc, to coordinate the Latin American and Caribbean left and debate alternatives to neoliberal economic policies.
founding.attendance: 48 parties and organizations from 14 Latin American and Caribbean countries.

formation.title: Origins & formative networks
formation.note: The Foro de São Paulo grew out of the Latin American left of the 1980s — socialist and communist parties, trade unions, guerrilla movements turning to electoral politics, and Christian currents. In Brazil, the Workers' Party (PT), the Forum's convener, was itself built from a coalition of trade unionists, Marxists and Catholics of the Liberation Theology tradition (the Christian base communities, CEBs).

items.title: Liberation Theology as a formative current
items.text: Liberation Theology — the Latin American Catholic movement linking the Gospel to social and political liberation — was one of the streams feeding the PT and the broader regional left that later convened the Forum. Clerics such as the Dominican friar Frei Betto and the theologian Leonardo Boff bridged the Catholic left, the PT, and revolutionary governments such as Cuba's.

items.title: Frei Betto — bridge to Cuba
items.text: Frei Betto (Carlos Alberto Libânio Christo), a Dominican friar and Liberation Theology figure, was a spiritual adviser to Lula and held long interviews with Fidel Castro that became the 1985 book 'Fidel and Religion' (Fidel e a Religião). He is widely credited in Brazilian accounts with brokering Lula's relationship with Fidel — the specific 'introduction' is reported in those accounts rather than independently documented here.

items.title: 1985 Havana debt conference — an early Lula–Fidel encounter
items.text: Lula first travelled to Cuba in 1985 for a Havana conference convened by Cuba on the Latin American foreign-debt crisis, with broad political, religious and social participation — five years before the Forum's 1990 founding. It is among the early contacts between the Brazilian left and Havana that prefigured the Forum's networks.

organization.note: The Forum has no permanent headquarters; coordination rotates among member-party apparatuses on a largely volunteer basis. The figures below are reported by the Forum and its affiliated sources and are still to be independently verified.

bodies.name: Executive Secretariat (Secretaria Executiva)
bodies.detail: Implements the decisions of the plenaries; reported as based in São Paulo and held by Brazil's PT.

bodies.name: Working Group (Grupo de Trabalho)
bodies.detail: Standing body with representation from about 16 countries, meeting periodically between the annual plenaries.

bodies.name: Regional Secretariat — Cone Sul
bodies.detail: Southern Cone regional secretariat; seat reported in Uruguay.

bodies.name: Regional Secretariat — Andino-Amazônica
bodies.detail: Andean–Amazonian regional secretariat; provisional seat reported in Colombia.

bodies.name: Regional Secretariat — Mesoamericana e Caribenha
bodies.detail: Mesoamerican & Caribbean regional secretariat; seat reported in El Salvador.

organization.scale: The PT reports about 123 member parties across 27 countries; the Forum says more than 100 parties and organizations participate. The 2023 Brasília meeting drew 700+ in-person and virtual registrants.

relatedOrganizations.name: Grupo de Puebla (Puebla Group)
relatedOrganizations.composition: Individual progressive leaders — presidents, ex-presidents, ministers, parliamentarians and intellectuals — rather than political parties.
relatedOrganizations.relationToForum: A distinct, complementary organization — NOT a renaming of the Foro de São Paulo. Launched in 2019 with the help of Foro-aligned networks; it notably does not include parties from Venezuela, Cuba and Bolivia, partly to distance itself from the authoritarian-left image. Both organizations remain active and have met side by side, e.g. in Tegucigalpa, June 2024.

relatedOrganizations.name: Progressive International
relatedOrganizations.composition: Global network of left/progressive movements, parties and figures.
relatedOrganizations.relationToForum: Allied international network; co-present with the Foro and the Puebla Group at the June 2024 Tegucigalpa gatherings. Separate organization with a worldwide (not Latin America–specific) scope.

relatedOrganizations.name: CELAC Social
relatedOrganizations.composition: Social-movements space associated with the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC), an intergovernmental body.
relatedOrganizations.relationToForum: Allied civil-society space, distinct from the Foro (which is a party forum, not an intergovernmental one). Co-present at the June 2024 Tegucigalpa gatherings.

criticalPerspectives.note: Several authors and outlets analyze the Foro de São Paulo as a coordinating network of the Latin American left, tracking the connections between its member parties and the spread of left governments in the region. These works are influential in Brazil's political debate. Some specific claims (e.g. formal ties to armed groups, or direct control of governments) are debated; such claims are attributed to their authors rather than asserted here as established fact.

works.author: Olavo de Carvalho
works.work: O Foro de São Paulo: A ascensão do comunismo latino-americano
works.thesis: A long-time analyst of the FSP, Carvalho argued it functions as a coordinated project advancing the Latin American left, and traced links between its member parties and movements — including, in his account, armed groups such as the FARC and Chile's MIR. He was central to bringing the FSP into Brazilian public debate; the strongest of these claims are debated. Much of this analysis was published through his outlet Mídia Sem Máscara (2002–2014, since revived), which also circulated a compiled “Atas do Foro de São Paulo”.

works.author: Graça Salgueiro
works.work: O Foro de São Paulo: A mais perigosa organização revolucionária das Américas
works.thesis: Argues the FSP is a far-reaching revolutionary network operating across the Americas, including through influence over media. Developed in her book and on her Rádio Vox program Observatório Latino.

works.author: Heitor De Paola
works.work: Commentary on the FSP, the 'Latin American axis' and the New World Order
works.thesis: Analyzes the FSP within a wider regional and geopolitical strategy of the left ('the Latin American axis').

membersInGovernment.note: Parties that belong to or are aligned with the Foro de São Paulo have held the presidency across much of Latin America — a measure of the network's electoral weight. (The region has also elected non-FSP, right-leaning governments, so this is a pattern, not exclusive control.) Founding/membership status of some parties is still being verified (see parties list).

armedMovements.note: The Forum was founded as a gathering of the whole Latin American left, and its participants included not only electoral parties but organizations that had waged, or still waged, armed struggle. Some — the FSLN in Nicaragua, the FMLN in El Salvador, the URNG in Guatemala, the MLN-Tupamaros in Uruguay — were guerrilla movements that became legal parties (the first two are listed among the parties above). Others took part as active armed organizations, most notably Colombia’s FARC and Chile’s MIR. Several of these groups were formally designated terrorist organizations by governments including the United States and the European Union; those designations are noted below with attribution. The precise extent and formality of each armed group’s participation in specific Forum meetings is documented unevenly, so those points are marked to verify and, where contested, attributed rather than asserted.
armedMovements.presidencyNote: A claim in circulation holds that “the FARC elected a president.” This conflates two distinct groups. The FARC’s successor party, Comunes, holds seats guaranteed by the 2016 peace accord in Colombia’s Congress but has never won the presidency. Colombia’s president elected in 2022, Gustavo Petro, is a former member of a different, earlier-demobilized guerrilla movement — the M-19 — and was the first former guerrilla to win the Colombian presidency.

movements.name: Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia — Ejército del Pueblo
movements.nature: The hemisphere’s longest-running Marxist–Leninist guerrilla insurgency; during the conflict it financed itself partly through kidnapping-for-ransom and the taxation of the cocaine trade.
movements.designation: Designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization by the United States (1997) and listed as a terrorist organization by the European Union; treated as such by successive Colombian governments during the armed conflict.
movements.fspRole: Took part in Foro de São Paulo encuentros during the 1990s and 2000s, when the Forum brought together armed and electoral currents of the left.
movements.currentStatus: Signed the 2016 peace accord and demobilized; in 2017 became a legal party — the Fuerza Alternativa Revolucionaria del Común, which kept the “FARC” acronym — renamed Comunes in 2021. The accord guarantees it 10 congressional seats for the 2018–2026 terms. It has not won the presidency.

movements.name: Movimiento de Izquierda Revolucionaria
movements.nature: Revolutionary-socialist movement that took up armed struggle, especially in clandestine resistance to the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990).
movements.designation: Repressed as a subversive organization by the Chilean military regime; many of its members were killed, disappeared or exiled.
movements.fspRole: Took part in early Foro de São Paulo meetings.
movements.currentStatus: Effectively defunct as an armed force after the return to democracy; only small successor groupings remain.

movements.name: Movimiento 19 de Abril
movements.nature: Nationalist, left-wing urban guerrilla, known for the 1980 Dominican embassy siege and the 1985 storming of the Palace of Justice in Bogotá.
movements.designation: Treated as a terrorist/subversive organization by the Colombian state during its armed period.
movements.fspRole: Demobilized in 1990 — the year the Forum was founded — and continued in legal politics through the Alianza Democrática M-19.
movements.currentStatus: Demobilized 1990. Former members stayed active in politics; Gustavo Petro, elected President of Colombia in 2022, is a former M-19 member.

movements.name: Movimiento de Liberación Nacional–Tupamaros
movements.nature: Urban guerrilla movement crushed under the 1973–1985 dictatorship, its members imprisoned for years.
movements.designation: Prosecuted as a subversive/terrorist organization under the Uruguayan dictatorship.
movements.fspRole: Joined the Frente Amplio — a founding-era Forum member — and takes part through it.
movements.currentStatus: Legal; part of the Frente Amplio coalition. José Mujica, a former Tupamaro imprisoned during the dictatorship, was President of Uruguay (2010–2015).

movements.name: Unidad Revolucionaria Nacional Guatemalteca
movements.nature: Coalition of Guatemalan guerrilla organizations during the civil war (1960–1996).
movements.designation: Treated as an insurgent/terrorist coalition by the Guatemalan state during the war.
movements.fspRole: Signed the 1996 peace accords and became a legal party; participant in the Forum.
